Welcome to St Laurence CofE Junior Academy.
St Laurence is a nurturing and inclusive junior school for children in Years 3 to 6. We are proud to provide a caring and supportive environment where every child is known as an individual, encouraged to grow in confidence and inspired to achieve their very best. Alongside high-quality teaching and learning, we place great importance on children’s wellbeing, personal development and sense of belonging. Our strong pastoral support, wonderful outdoor spaces and opportunities such as Forest School help children to develop resilience, independence and a lasting love of learning.
Explore our website to keep up to date with school events, access useful resources and find out more about daily life at St Laurence. Parents and carers can find important information, celebrate children’s learning and stay connected with their child’s educational journey. Prospective parents and visitors are warmly invited to discover the values, opportunities and sense of community that make our school a special place to learn and grow.
Our School Vision
Our school is a supportive and inclusive community where every person is known, found and loved. Through an inspiring and aspirational curriculum, we enable each child to grow in knowledge, skills and character, becoming hopeful, joyful and resilient learners who flourish now and in the future. With forgiveness, fresh starts and strong relationships, we foster a community where all are valued.
Through an aspirational and engaging curriculum, children are encouraged to develop their knowledge, skills and character. We aim to inspire curiosity, build resilience and nurture a love of learning, empowering every child to reach their full potential both now and into the future.

A Week of Reading at St Laurence
This week, pupils at St Laurence-in-Thanet CE Junior Academy enjoyed a fantastic celebration of reading as part of our World Book Day events. The week began with a special reading exchange with Ellington Infant School, where pupils from both schools visited each other to share and enjoy stories together. On Tuesday, the children took part in creative writing workshops with Wizard Stories, using music, humour and imagination to inspire their own storytelling. We were also delighted to welcome Nicci from Happy Reading Children’s Bookshop, who brought a selection of books so pupils could collect their World Book Day books and take them home. The week finished with our Pirates and Fairytales dress-up day on Thursday, with pupils and staff arriving in a wonderful range of costumes. It was a brilliant week celebrating the joy of books and reading across the school.
Chinese Dance Workshop
Each class were fortunate to take part in an exciting Chinese dance workshop. During the session, pupils learned about Chinese New Year, which took place on 17 February, and explored some of the traditions associated with the celebration. The children discovered the story behind the first dragon dance and learned why masks and lanterns are an important part of the festivities. They then had the opportunity to try some traditional dance movements themselves, bringing the stories and traditions to life.
New Sensory Room!!
Our new sensory room has now been installed! It has taken a year to move from the initial idea to completion and we are delighted with the finished space. Thank you to the charities and organisations whose generous funding made this possible. Children will begin using the room from September.

What Maths looks like at St LaurenceAt St Laurence, we believe that Mathematics is essential for everyday life. Our curriculum develops confident, curious and resilient mathematicians who understand that Maths is not simply about completing calculations, but about exploring patterns, making connections, explaining ideas and solving problems.
We want children to recognise how Mathematics is used in daily life, financial literacy, future employment and the wider world. We also want them to experience Maths as an enjoyable, engaging and rewarding subject.
We follow the National Curriculum for Mathematics and use White Rose Maths to support the planning and sequencing of lessons. Children receive varied and frequent opportunities to practise their skills, develop secure conceptual understanding and apply their knowledge accurately and efficiently.
Our curriculum aimsThrough our Maths curriculum, children will:• become fluent in the fundamentals of Mathematics• develop secure conceptual understanding• recall and apply important facts accurately and efficiently• reason mathematically using appropriate vocabulary• describe, explain, convince, justify and prove their ideas• solve routine and non-routine problems• identify patterns and make connections• select appropriate strategies and representations• apply mathematical knowledge to everyday situations• approach challenges with confidence, curiosity and perseverance
How we teach MathsMaths is taught through carefully sequenced lessons which build upon children’s previous knowledge and understanding.Teachers use clear explanations, modelling, practical resources and visual representations to introduce and explore mathematical concepts. Children move between concrete resources, pictorial representations and abstract mathematical notation so that they understand both how and why a method works.
Lessons include a balance of:• fluency and calculation• mathematical reasoning• problem-solving• practical exploration• discussion and explanation• independent work• paired and collaborative learning• retrieval and regular practice
Children are expected to use mathematical vocabulary when discussing their ideas. They are encouraged to explain their methods, compare different approaches and provide evidence to support their conclusions.
Previously taught knowledge is revisited regularly so that children retain important facts and can apply them confidently in different contexts.
Our mastery approachWe use a mastery approach to the teaching of Mathematics. This means that children are given sufficient time to explore and understand a concept before moving on to new learning.
The majority of pupils move through the programmes of study at broadly the same pace. Teachers use appropriate scaffolding, resources and targeted support to ensure that all children can access the learning while maintaining ambitious expectations.
Decisions about when to move on are based on the security of children’s understanding and their readiness for the next stage.Children who grasp a concept quickly are challenged through rich and increasingly sophisticated reasoning and problem-solving tasks rather than being moved prematurely onto new content. Children who require further support receive additional explanation, modelling, practice and opportunities to consolidate earlier learning.
Fluency, reasoning and problem-solving
Fluency, reasoning and problem-solving are central to every part of our Maths curriculum.
FluencyFluency involves much more than remembering facts. Children develop secure knowledge of mathematical relationships and become increasingly accurate and efficient when choosing and applying methods.
Regular practice helps pupils recall important facts quickly, freeing them to concentrate on more complex reasoning and problem-solving.
ReasoningChildren are taught to follow a line of enquiry, identify relationships and explain their mathematical thinking.They learn to:• describe what they notice• explain how they reached an answer• compare different methods• convince others that an idea is correct• justify their decisions• prove or disprove mathematical statements
Problem-solvingChildren apply their knowledge to a variety of familiar and unfamiliar problems. They learn to break complex problems into smaller steps, select suitable strategies, identify relevant information and persevere when the solution is not immediately clear.
They learn to break complex problems into smaller steps, select suitable strategies, identify relevant information and persevere when the solution is not immediately clear.
Mathematical vocabularyMathematical vocabulary is taught explicitly as an essential part of every lesson.
Children need to understand the vocabulary associated with the area of Mathematics they are studying and use it accurately when explaining their thinking.
Teachers model appropriate language and provide opportunities for pupils to discuss patterns, relationships, methods and conclusions. Children are encouraged to make connections between vocabulary used in different areas of Mathematics.
Developing secure mathematical language helps children explain their reasoning, understand questions and participate confidently in mathematical discussions.
What children learnThroughout Key Stage 2, children develop their knowledge, fluency and confidence across the main areas of Mathematics.• Number and place value• Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division• Fractions, decimals and percentages• Measurement• Geometry• Statistics• Algebra
Times tablesSecure knowledge of multiplication and division facts is crucial to children’s progress in Mathematics.Times tables support learning across many areas, including:• written multiplication and division• fractions• decimals• percentages• ratio• area• problem-solving
Children who can recall these facts quickly are able to concentrate more fully on the reasoning and processes required within increasingly complex tasks.
We place a strong emphasis on times tables throughout the school and use Times Tables Rock Stars to support regular practice. This enjoyable and challenging programme encourages children to develop rapid and accurate recall through frequent rehearsal.
Supporting times tables at home
Regular, short periods of practice are usually more effective than occasional longer sessions.Families can support children by:• practising one times table at a time• asking multiplication and related division questions• looking for patterns within tables• using Times Tables Rock Stars• playing times table games• practising in a different order rather than always beginning at one• discussing which facts children already know and which require more practice
Parents can also access our Parents’ Guide to Times Tables and the Parents’ Guide to Times Tables Rock Stars for further ideas and support.
The Multiplication Tables CheckChildren in Year 4 complete the statutory Multiplication Tables Check.
The purpose of the check is to determine whether pupils can fluently recall their multiplication tables up to 12 × 12. Secure recall supports children’s future success across the Mathematics curriculum.
Throughout Key Stage 2, children are given regular opportunities to develop their speed, accuracy and confidence before completing the check.
Key Instant Recall FactsTo develop children’s fluency and mental calculation skills, we use Key Instant Recall Facts, known as KIRFs, throughout the school.KIRFs are important facts which children learn by heart so that they can recall them quickly and accurately. These may include:• number bonds• multiplication facts• division facts• doubles and halves• fraction, decimal and percentage relationships• facts involving measures and time
These facts underpin much of the Mathematics curriculum. Secure recall allows children to work more efficiently when completing mental and written calculations and when solving more complex problems.
Each half term, children focus on a particular KIRF in school. This is also shared with families so that it can be practised regularly at home.
Frequent practice for short periods is particularly effective. By developing instant recall, children become more confident with number work and are better able to access the wider Maths curriculum.
By the end of Year 6By the end of Key Stage 2, children will be able to:• recall and apply important number facts accurately and efficiently• use appropriate mental and written calculation methods• demonstrate secure conceptual understanding• select appropriate strategies for different tasks• use mathematical vocabulary confidently• explain and justify their methods• identify patterns and mathematical relationships• make connections between different areas of Mathematics• solve increasingly complex routine and non-routine problems• check whether their answers are reasonable• interpret and present mathematical information• apply Mathematics to everyday situations• approach mathematical challenges with confidence and resilience
Enrichment and wider opportunitiesChildren are encouraged to recognise and apply Mathematics beyond their usual Maths lessons. Opportunities may include:• mathematical games and investigations• practical challenges• problem-solving activities• times tables competitions• applying Maths through Science• collecting and interpreting data• measuring within Design and Technology• using coordinates and scale in Geography• exploring financial literacy• using Mathematics within Computing
These experiences help pupils understand that Mathematics is relevant, useful and present throughout everyday life.
Supporting all learnersOur Maths curriculum is adapted so that every child can participate, make progress and experience success.Teachers may use:• practical equipment and manipulatives• visual representations• worked examples• vocabulary support• smaller steps• repeated modelling• additional rehearsal• carefully structured questions• multiplication grids or number lines where appropriate• paired discussion• pre-teaching and intervention
Children who need further support are given opportunities to revisit and consolidate their understanding. Pupils who are secure deepen their learning by reasoning, making connections and applying their knowledge to increasingly sophisticated problems.
Adaptations are used to provide access to the same ambitious curriculum rather than unnecessarily limiting the mathematical content children experience.
Personal and spiritual developmentMathematics encourages children to be curious, thoughtful and persistent.
Children experience a sense of wonder as they explore patterns, relationships and the order found within numbers, shapes and the wider world.
They learn that challenges can be overcome through patience, careful thinking and a willingness to try a different approach. Working with others also helps children to listen respectfully, explain their ideas and recognise that a problem may be solved in more than one way.
Through Mathematics, pupils develop resilience and confidence, understanding that mistakes are a valuable part of learning.
Supporting Maths at homeFamilies play an important role in developing children’s confidence and positive attitudes towards Mathematics.
Maths can be brought to life through ordinary activities at home and in the community. These everyday experiences help children understand why mathematical knowledge is useful.
Maths moments at home
Families can support mathematical learning by:• using money when shopping• comparing prices and calculating change• reading clocks and timetables• measuring ingredients when cooking• estimating distances and quantities• measuring objects and spaces• discussing shapes and patterns• planning journeys• sharing items equally• calculating scores during games• discussing fractions when cutting or sharing food
The most helpful conversations often involve asking children how they reached an answer rather than simply checking whether the answer is correct.
Games can make mathematical practice enjoyable and motivating.
Board games, card games and puzzles help children become more familiar with numbers, patterns, counting and strategy. They also develop concentration, turn-taking, reasoning and problem-solving.
Children make the strongest progress when important skills are revisited regularly until they become secure. Games provide a purposeful and enjoyable context for this repeated practice.
Oxford Owl Maths support
Oxford Owl provides advice for families about supporting Mathematics at home.The website includes:• explanations of primary Maths terminology• guidance about what children learn at school• games and activity ideas• suggestions for developing mathematical confidence• support with calculations and mathematical methods
Online Maths activities
We use a range of online games and activities to support mathematical learning. Families may also find the following resources useful:Topmarks problem-solving gamesBBC Bite Maths Hit the ButtonTeaching TablesMaths GamesMaths ZoneMaths Is FunTimesTables.co.ukMultiplication Tables Check practice tool
Online games should support, rather than replace, discussion, practical experiences and regular opportunities to apply Mathematics in everyday life. The current page provides direct links to each of these resources.

What Music looks like at St LaurenceAt St Laurence, our Music curriculum gives every child the opportunity to sing, listen, compose, perform and develop a lasting appreciation of music.
Children explore music from different periods, traditions, cultures and genres. They learn about significant composers, performers and musicians from the past and present while developing their own creativity, confidence and musical understanding.
We use Charanga to support the planning and teaching of Music. The curriculum is carefully sequenced so that children revisit and develop their knowledge and skills as they progress through Key Stage 2.
Our curriculum aimsThrough our Music curriculum, children will:• enjoy listening to and making music• sing confidently, expressively and with increasing control• perform using their voices and a range of instruments• improvise and compose their own music• listen carefully and respond to different musical styles• develop an understanding of rhythm, pitch, tempo, dynamics, texture and structure• use appropriate musical vocabulary• learn about significant composers, performers and musical traditions• develop confidence, creativity and teamwork
How we teach MusicMusic is taught through practical and engaging lessons using Charanga. Children listen, sing, play, improvise, compose and perform during each unit. Lessons provide opportunities for children to:• learn and perform songs• play tuned and untuned instruments• follow rhythms and musical notation• improvise short musical ideas• compose individually and collaboratively• listen to and appraise a wide range of music• rehearse and refine performances• discuss music using appropriate vocabulary
Children explore a broad range of musical styles and genres, including rock, pop, hip-hop and Motown. They use instruments such as glockenspiels, xylophones, recorders, keyboards and ocarinas during their lessons.
What children learnThroughout Key Stage 2, children develop their knowledge and confidence across the main areas of Music.• Singing• Listening and appraising• Performing• Improvising• Composing• Musical notation
Learning an instrumentThroughout their time at St Laurence, children have opportunities to learn and perform using a range of instruments.
Children in Years 3 and 5 receive weekly ukulele lessons from a specialist music teacher. These lessons help pupils develop instrumental technique, rhythm, musical notation and ensemble skills. Our aim is for every child to have the opportunity to learn at least one musical instrument during their time at the school.
By the end of Year 6By the end of Key Stage 2, children will be able to:• sing with increasing accuracy, confidence and expression• maintain their part when performing with others• play a range of instruments with increasing control• listen attentively and identify important musical features• use musical vocabulary to describe and compare music• improvise within a given structure• compose and refine their own musical ideas• use and interpret simple musical notation• discuss music from different periods, genres and cultures• rehearse, perform and evaluate their work• contribute confidently and respectfully to an ensemble
Enrichment and wider opportunitiesMusic is an important part of life at St Laurence and children are given opportunities to perform beyond their usual lessons.
Year 4 pupils take part in Young Voices at the O2 Arena in London. This memorable experience gives children the opportunity to sing and perform as part of a large choir, developing their confidence, teamwork and enjoyment of music.
Additional musical opportunities include:• choir• guitar club• performances in school• collective worship and celebrations• specialist instrumental tuition• individual music lessons• opportunities to perform to families and the wider community
These experiences allow children to develop their skills, celebrate their achievements and experience the enjoyment of making music with others.
Supporting all learnersOur Music curriculum is adapted so that every child can participate, make progress and experience success.
Teachers may use visual prompts, repeated listening, simplified instrumental parts, colour-coded notation, modelling and opportunities for additional rehearsal. Children can contribute through singing, playing, composing, listening or responding in different ways.
Instruments and activities can be adapted to meet children’s physical, sensory and communication needs while maintaining ambitious expectations for all.
Personal and spiritual developmentMusic gives children opportunities to experience joy, wonder, reflection and a sense of belonging.
Listening to and performing music can help pupils express emotions, consider experiences beyond their own and appreciate beauty and creativity. Exploring music from different cultures and traditions also develops respect and curiosity about the wider world.
Performing together teaches children to listen carefully, value the contribution of others and understand that each person plays an important part in creating something meaningful.

Our commitment is to provide a challenging, and well-structured curriculum offering various pathways, ensuring an engaging and rigorous education for students of all capabilities.The key objectives for our curriculum include:Catering to the individual needs of our students.Attaining the best possible academic outcomes for every student.Ensuring enduring high-quality learning experiences.Facilitating substantive and disciplinary knowledge, oracy and language acquisition.Cultivating transferrable skills development.Preparing students for the subsequent stages of education, employment and life in contemporary Britain.Fostering the development of well-rounded, confident and open-minded young adultOur teaching strategies are grounded in metacognitive and retrieval practice pedagogies. What Physical Education looks like at St LaurenceAt St Laurence, our Physical Education curriculum enables children to become confident, active and physically literate. We want pupils to enjoy movement, develop healthy habits and recognise the important role physical activity plays in their wellbeing.
Our curriculum develops physical skills alongside teamwork, communication, resilience and decision-making. Children learn how to apply themselves when working individually, as part of a team and in competitive situations.
We use The PE Hub to support the planning and teaching of Physical Education. Lessons are carefully sequenced so that children progressively develop their knowledge, vocabulary, techniques and understanding across Key Stage 2.
Our curriculum aimsThrough our Physical Education curriculum, children will:• develop competence and confidence in a broad range of physical activities• improve their strength, flexibility, balance, control and coordination• understand how different skills can be transferred between sports• develop tactical awareness and make effective decisions• communicate and work successfully with others• evaluate performance and identify ways to improve• experience individual and team competition• understand the importance of warming up and cooling down safely• recognise the benefits of regular physical activity• develop positive attitudes towards health and active lifestyles
How we teach Physical EducationPhysical Education is taught through carefully planned, practical lessons which allow children to develop and apply their skills.Teachers use clear explanations, demonstrations and subject-specific vocabulary. Children practise techniques, take part in increasingly challenging activities and reflect on their own performance and that of others.Our approach considers the whole child through the principles of thinking, behaving and doing.
ThinkingChildren learn to:• select and combine skills effectively• make tactical decisions• identify ways to improve• evaluate their own performance• recognise successful strategies
BehavingChildren learn to:• communicate and collaborate• compete fairly• follow rules• show respect towards others• respond appropriately to winning and losing• take responsibility within a team
DoingChildren learn to:• perform a broad range of movements and skills• develop strength, flexibility, technique, control and balance• apply skills in different situations• improve through practice, feedback and perseverance
This reflects the existing Head, Heart and Hands approach while using clearer language for families.
What children learnThroughout Key Stage 2, children experience seven fundamental areas of Physical Education alongside swimming.• Athletics• Invasion games• Striking and fielding games• Net and wall games• Outdoor and adventurous activities• Dance• Gymnastics• Swimming• Competition and school sport
Competition is an important part of Physical Education and school life at St Laurence.
Children experience appropriate competitive situations during lessons and may take part in a competition or performance at the end of a unit. They also compete against their own previous achievements through personal-best challenges.
Pupils have opportunities to represent their houses in events such as cross-country and Sports Day. Children may also be selected to represent St Laurence in competitions against other schools, including events organised through our Thanet PASSPORT membership.
Representing the school is an honour. We expect pupils to demonstrate courage, respect, teamwork and good sportsmanship, whatever the outcome.
Physical activity throughout the school dayWe encourage children to be active beyond their formal Physical Education lessons.Opportunities include:• the Daily Mile• active play during break and lunchtime• playground games and equipment• after-school sports clubs• house competitions• activities and movement across the wider curriculum
These opportunities help children to understand that physical activity should be a regular and enjoyable part of everyday life.
By the end of Year 6By the end of Key Stage 2, children will be able to:• perform a broad range of physical skills with increasing control• apply techniques effectively across different activities• make thoughtful tactical decisions• explain how skills can transfer between sports• work collaboratively and communicate effectively• evaluate performance and suggest improvements• lead and support others during physical activities• understand and follow the rules of a range of sports• warm up and cool down safely• compete respectfully and respond positively to winning and losing• understand how physical activity supports health and wellbeing• approach new physical challenges with confidence and resilience
Enrichment and wider opportunitiesChildren are given opportunities to participate in a range of sporting and physical activities beyond their normal lessons.These may include:• inter-house competitions• Sports Day• cross-country events• after-school clubs• coaching sessions and workshops• competitions against other schools• activities provided through Thanet PASSPORT• leadership opportunities for older pupils
These experiences help children discover new interests, develop confidence and experience the enjoyment of belonging to a team.
Supporting all learnersOur Physical Education curriculum is adapted so that every child can participate, make progress and experience success.Teachers may adapt equipment, playing areas, rules, group s, movement expectations or the level of support provided. Skills are broken into manageable stages and children are given suitable opportunities to practise and consolidate their learning.
Adaptations are made thoughtfully so that children can participate alongside their peers while maintaining appropriate challenge and ambition.
Personal and spiritual developmentPhysical Education teaches children the importance of fairness, courage, self-discipline and respect.
Pupils learn to recognise their own strengths, respond positively to setbacks and encourage others. They experience the joy of movement, the satisfaction of improvement and the sense of belonging that comes from working towards a shared goal.
Through competition and collaboration, children learn that success is not only measured by winning. It can also be found in perseverance, personal improvement, teamwork and showing respect towards others.
Supporting Physical Education at homeFamilies can encourage active and healthy lifestyles through simple activities such as:• walking, cycling or scooting• visiting parks and outdoor spaces• playing active games together• practising throwing, catching and balancing• joining a local sports club• setting personal activity challenges• discussing the importance of rest, nutrition and hydration
Regular opportunities to move and play can help children build confidence, develop healthy habits and enjoy being active.

What PSHE and RSE look like at St LaurenceAt St Laurence, Personal, Social, Health and Economic education is an important part of our whole curriculum and everyday school life.
Our PSHE curriculum helps children to develop the knowledge, skills and understanding they need to lead confident, healthy and independent lives. It prepares them for the opportunities, responsibilities and experiences they face now and as they grow older.
We use Kapow Primary to support the planning and teaching of PSHE and Relationships and Sex Education. Learning is carefully sequenced so that children revisit important themes and develop increasingly mature understanding throughout Key Stage 2.
Our curriculum aimsThrough our PSHE and RSE curriculum, children will:• develop positive relationships with others• understand and manage their emotions• recognise their own strengths and qualities• make informed and responsible choices• understand how to keep themselves physically and emotionally healthy• recognise safe and unsafe situations• know when and how to seek help• respect differences between people• understand that actions and choices have consequences• develop the skills needed to become responsible and active citizens
How we teach PSHE and RSEPSHE is taught through regular lessons as well as through wider school life, collective worship, pastoral support and opportunities for pupil leadership.
Lessons provide a safe and supportive environment in which children can explore ideas, ask questions and consider different situations. Teachers establish clear expectations so that pupils can participate respectfully without being expected to share personal information.
Teaching may include:• class discussion• stories and scenarios• role play• paired and group activities• reflection• problem-solving tasks• practical activities• opportunities to consider different viewpoints
Children are taught to listen carefully, disagree respectfully and recognise that people may have different experiences, beliefs and family circumstances.
What children learnThroughout Key Stage 2, children develop their understanding across the main areas of PSHE and RSE.• Families and relationships• Health and wellbeing• Safety and the changing body• Citizenship• Economic wellbeing• Transition and personal development
Relationships and Sex EducationRelationships Education is statutory in primary schools and forms an integral part of our PSHE curriculum.
Children learn about caring friendships, respectful relationships, families, personal boundaries and how to seek help when something does not feel right.
Sex Education is taught in an age-appropriate and sensitive manner, following the school’s agreed RSE Policy. Teaching builds upon learning in Science and helps pupils understand changes associated with growing up and puberty.
Families are informed about the content of the curriculum and can find further information in our RSE Policy.
Keeping children safeAn important part of PSHE is helping children recognise how to keep themselves and others safe. Children learn about:• trusted adults and support networks• personal boundaries and consent• safe and unsafe secrets• responding to peer pressure• basic first aid and emergencies• road, water and fire safety• online safety• harmful substances• recognising worrying behaviour• reporting concerns and asking for help
Key safety messages are revisited regularly and taught in language appropriate to the children’s age and stage of development.
By the end of Year 6By the end of Key Stage 2, children will be able to:• recognise the features of healthy and respectful relationships• communicate their feelings, needs and boundaries appropriately• identify strategies for managing emotions and setbacks• make informed choices about their health and wellbeing• recognise risks and know how to seek support• understand physical and emotional changes associated with growing up• respect differences between people and families• understand their rights and responsibilities• make thoughtful decisions about money• contribute positively to their school and wider community• approach transition with increasing confidence and independence
Enrichment and wider opportunitiesChildren develop their personal and social skills through a wide range of experiences beyond individual PSHE lessons.These may include:• School Council and Eco Warriors• Worship Shepherds• House Captains and prefect roles• charitable and community projects• Agents of Change activities• workshops and visitors• online safety activities• mental health and wellbeing events• transition activities• residential visits and educational trips
These opportunities help children practise leadership, teamwork, responsibility and active citizenship.
Supporting mental health and wellbeingPSHE forms part of our wider approach to supporting children’s mental health and emotional wellbeing.
Children are taught to recognise and name emotions, identify strategies that may help them regulate and understand that everybody needs support at times. They learn how trusted adults, friendships, routines and healthy choices can contribute to wellbeing.
Our wider provision includes approaches and support such as Thrive, Zones of Regulation, ELSA and nurture-based interventions for children who may benefit from additional help.
Supporting all learnersOur PSHE curriculum is adapted so that every child can participate safely, make progress and experience success.
Teachers may use visual supports, carefully chosen vocabulary, social stories, role play, pre-teaching and opportunities to revisit learning. Sensitive topics are introduced thoughtfully and adapted to children’s developmental and communication needs.
Where appropriate, staff work with families and other professionals to ensure that teaching is accessible, respectful and suitable for individual pupils.
Personal and spiritual developmentPSHE encourages children to reflect on who they are, how they relate to others and the contribution they can make to their community.
Children consider questions of identity, belonging, fairness, responsibility and compassion. They learn to recognise the value of every person and understand the importance of treating others with dignity and respect.
Through discussion, reflection and practical action, pupils develop the confidence and character needed to become hopeful, joyful and resilient members of their communities.

ST LAURENCE-IN-THANET
CE JUNIOR ACADEMY
At St Laurence-in-Thanet CE Junior Academy, we strongly believe that possessing comprehensive information about a child is crucial in determining the most appropriate support for them. Regular collaboration with various external agencies is a cornerstone of our approach, and we highly value the guidance they provide.Prior to referring a child to an external agency for advice on their additional needs, we actively seek and respect parental consent. Encouraging parents to permit agencies to share information with a designated staff member at school is an integral part of our collaborative effort.Our experienced school staff benefit from the support provided by numerous organisations, including but not limited to:• Occupational Therapists• Speech and Language Therapists• Specialist Teaching and Learning Service (TISS)• Educational Psychologists• NELFT Emotional Wellbeing Team• School Nursing Team• NELFT NHS Foundation Trust• Child Counsellors• Early Help Team• Social Services
In-house assessments are conducted during a child's time at St Laurence-in-Thanet CE Junior Academy. These assessments, initiated at the request of the class teacher, help identify students requiring further intervention in literacy and numeracy or those with specific learning needs. Some of the assessments carried out by trained staff include:• IDL Literacy screener• IDL Numeracy screener• Visual Stress Test• A range of assessments for maths difficulties• Boxall Profile/Thrive assessment
Parents or carers with concerns about their child’s educational needs are encouraged to initially discuss them with their child’s teacher. If further guidance is needed, the school’s SENCO is available and happy to assist.

CE JUNIOR ACADEMY
What History looks like at St LaurenceAt St Laurence, our History curriculum develops children’s curiosity about the past and helps them to understand how people, events and ideas have shaped the world in which they live.
Children study a broad range of historical periods, societies and significant individuals. They explore British, local and world history, building a secure sense of chronology while learning to recognise connections, contrasts and changes over time.
Our class names reflect our commitment to local history, with each class named after a significant historical figure who has links to Ramsgate. Through this, children develop a stronger understanding of the heritage of their local community as well as the wider world.
Our curriculum aimsThrough our History curriculum, children will:• develop a secure understanding of chronology• build a wide and accurate historical vocabulary• ask thoughtful questions about the past• examine evidence and consider its reliability• recognise different interpretations of historical events• understand cause, consequence, change, continuity, similarity and difference• learn about British, local and world history• develop confidence in researching and presenting historical ideas• understand how the past has influenced life today
How we teach HistoryHistory is taught through carefully planned units organised around an overarching enquiry question. Each enquiry encourages children to investigate the past, examine evidence and reach conclusions based on what they have discovered. Teachers introduce key historical knowledge and vocabulary while helping pupils to develop the skills of a historian.
Children regularly revisit important concepts so that their understanding becomes increasingly secure. These include:• chronology• cause and consequence• change and continuity• similarity and difference• historical significance• evidence• interpretation
Where appropriate, meaningful links are made with subjects such as English, Geography, Science and Art. For example, historical themes may inspire high-quality reading and writing while allowing children to deepen their understanding of a particular period.
Historical enquiryHistorical enquiry is central to our curriculum. Children are encouraged to ask questions, investigate sources and develop reasoned responses.They may work with:• written records• photographs and paintings• maps• artefacts• archaeological evidence• oral accounts• buildings and local landmarks• reconstructions and digital resources
Children learn that sources do not always provide a complete or neutral account of the past. As they progress through the school, they become increasingly confident in comparing evidence, considering different viewpoints and explaining how interpretations may vary.
What children learnThroughout Key Stage 2, children develop their knowledge and skills across British, local and world history.• Chronology• Change and continuity• Cause and consequence• Similarity and difference• Evidence and interpretation• Local history
By the end of Year 6By the end of Key Stage 2, children will be able to:• place significant periods and events in chronological order• use historical vocabulary accurately and confidently• explain causes, consequences, changes and connections• ask perceptive questions about the past• select and examine evidence from a range of sources• consider the reliability and usefulness of historical evidence• recognise that the past can be interpreted in different ways• construct informed responses supported by evidence• make connections between local, British and world history• explain how historical events and ideas continue to influence life today
Enrichment and wider opportunitiesWe enrich our History curriculum through memorable experiences that bring learning to life.
These include themed days, visits, workshops, practical activities and opportunities to explore local heritage. Previous experiences have included visits to Dover Museum, Kent Life and Ramsgate Tunnels, as well as VE Day activities, virtual reality workshops and practical tasks such as archaeological digs, making Egyptian bread and mummifying tomatoes.
These experiences provide valuable opportunities for children to handle evidence, ask questions and develop a deeper understanding of the periods they study.
We also work with other schools across the Aquila Trust to share good practice and strengthen the teaching and learning of History.
Supporting all learnersOur History curriculum is adapted so that every child can participate, make progress and experience success.
Teachers may use timelines, images, artefacts, vocabulary mats, maps, drama, practical activities and carefully structured written tasks. New knowledge is introduced in manageable steps and regularly revisited.
Children may demonstrate their understanding through discussion, diagrams, role play, presentations and practical work as well as extended writing. This allows pupils to engage with historical ideas in different ways while maintaining ambitious expectations for all.
Personal and spiritual developmentHistory helps children to understand the experiences, beliefs and perspectives of people whose lives may have been very different from their own.
Pupils consider questions of justice, power, conflict, courage and responsibility. They explore how individuals and communities have responded to challenge and change, developing empathy without judging the past only by modern standards.
Through local and world history, children gain a stronger sense of identity, belonging and their place within a much longer human story. They are encouraged to reflect thoughtfully on the lessons that can be learnt from the past.Click here to view the St Laurence History curriculum booklet

CE JUNIOR ACADEMY
What Geography looks like at St LaurenceAt St Laurence, our Geography curriculum inspires children to develop curiosity and fascination about the world around them. Through the study of people, places and environments, children gain an understanding of space, place and scale whilst developing an appreciation of how the world is connected.We teach children about their local area and encourage them to compare their experiences with those of people living in other regions of the United Kingdom and across the world. Through enquiry, investigation and fieldwork, pupils develop the knowledge, skills and vocabulary needed to understand both the human and physical features of our planet.
Our curriculum aimsThrough our Geography curriculum, children will:• develop curiosity and fascination about the world around them• gain a secure knowledge of where places are and what they are like• understand how places are similar and different• develop geographical vocabulary and subject knowledge• learn how human and physical processes shape environments• develop fieldwork skills and geographical techniques• use maps, atlases, aerial photographs and digital mapping tools effectively• understand current environmental and societal issues• make connections between people, places and environments• become informed and responsible global citizens
How we teach GeographyGeography is taught through carefully planned units built around engaging Enquiry Questions. These questions encourage children to investigate geographical concepts, think critically and apply their knowledge to real-world contexts.Lessons include a range of activities, including:• map work and atlas skills• fieldwork and observation• geographical enquiries and investigations• use of aerial photographs and satellite imagery• data collection and interpretation• research using a variety of sources• discussion and collaborative learning• opportunities to communicate findings and conclusions
Each term, teachers plan units that build progressively on previous learning. Key geographical knowledge, skills and vocabulary are revisited regularly to help children make connections and strengthen understanding.
Cross-curricular links are made wherever appropriate. For example, Year 5 children link their learning in Earth and Space with Geography through the use of satellite imagery and digital mapping equipment.
Through our enquiry approach, children learn to ask questions, gather evidence, draw conclusions and evaluate their understanding.
What children learnThroughout Key Stage 2, children progressively develop their knowledge and skills across the main areas of geography.• Locational knowledge• Place knowledge• Human geography• Physical geography• Geographical enquiry• Fieldwork• Mapping and data interpretation• Environmental awareness
By the end of Year 6By the end of Key Stage 2, children will be able to:• locate and describe a range of places and environments using geographical vocabulary• explain similarities and differences between locations and regions• understand key physical and human geographical processes• use maps, atlases, aerial photographs and digital technologies confidently• collect, analyse and present geographical information• carry out fieldwork investigations with increasing independence• understand the impact people have on environments and communities• discuss current geographical and environmental issues• communicate geographical understanding using appropriate terminology• apply their geographical knowledge to understand the wider world
Enrichment and wider opportunitiesChildren have opportunities to enrich their geographical learning through theme days, visits and practical experiences. Geography is brought to life through events such as Earth Day, educational visits and outdoor learning opportunities.
Visits may include locations such as Dover Museum, Kent Life and Ramsgate Harbour, while practical experiences such as map work, forest school activities and investigations help children develop their understanding beyond the classroom.
These memorable experiences provide meaningful contexts for learning and inspire children's curiosity about the world around them.
Supporting all learnersOur Geography curriculum is designed so that all children can access learning, make progress and experience success.
Teachers adapt lessons using visual resources, modelling, practical activities, vocabulary support, discussion opportunities and scaffolded tasks. Key concepts and vocabulary are introduced carefully and revisited regularly to ensure that all pupils can build secure understanding over time.
Children are encouraged to investigate, explore and share ideas with confidence in a supportive learning environment.
Personal and spiritual developmentGeography helps children develop a deeper understanding of the world and the people within it.
By learning about different countries, cultures and environments, pupils develop empathy, respect and appreciation for diversity. They learn about the challenges facing our planet and consider how their choices can impact local and global communities.
Geography encourages children to reflect on their place in the world, develop a sense of responsibility towards the environment and appreciate the interconnected nature of people's lives across the globe.

What English looks like at St LaurenceAt St Laurence, English is at the heart of our curriculum. Through reading, writing, speaking and listening, children develop the knowledge, confidence and communication skills they need to succeed across every subject and throughout their lives.
Our English curriculum is made up of several closely connected areas:• reading• phonics• writing• grammar and punctuation• spelling• speaking and listening
Although these areas are taught explicitly, they are brought together throughout the curriculum. Children read as writers, use discussion to develop their ideas and apply their knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, punctuation and spelling when communicating for different purposes.
Our curriculum aimsThrough our English curriculum, children will:• become confident, fluent and enthusiastic readers• develop a lifelong enjoyment of books and reading• understand and discuss a wide range of texts• write clearly, accurately and creatively for different purposes• develop a rich and varied vocabulary• speak confidently and listen respectfully• use grammar, punctuation and spelling accurately• organise and communicate their ideas effectively• reflect on, edit and improve their work• develop confidence, independence and resilience as communicators
What Reading looks like at St LaurenceReading is the cornerstone of learning at St Laurence and provides the foundation for success across the wider curriculum. We aim for every child to leave primary school as a confident and capable reader who enjoys books and understands how reading can help them discover new ideas, experiences and perspectives.
Children encounter a broad range of high-quality fiction, non-fiction, poetry, speeches and plays. Our carefully planned reading spine introduces pupils to different authors, cultures, genres and increasingly complex texts as they move through Key Stage 2.
Teachers regularly read aloud to their classes, allowing every child to experience rich and engaging literature. Books are selected to reflect children’s interests, support curriculum learning and introduce pupils to a diverse range of contemporary and established authors.
How we teach Reading
Whole Class ReadingWhole Class Reading sessions are based on carefully selected books, extracts and other high-quality texts. Children are explicitly taught the knowledge and strategies needed to understand increasingly complex material. Lessons develop children’s ability to:• retrieve information• explain ideas• make inferences• justify responses using evidence• predict what may happen• summarise information• explore vocabulary in context• consider an author’s choice of language• compare ideas, characters and texts• discuss different interpretations
Children are encouraged to express their views, listen carefully to others and return to the text to support their responses. Our reading spine ensures that pupils experience a carefully sequenced range of texts throughout Years 3 to 6. Alongside the core reading texts, each term includes a planned Readers Theatre text, including poetry, speeches, narrative extracts and performance pieces.
Readers TheatreReaders Theatre is an important part of our Reading and Oracy curriculum. Each term, children complete a two-week unit of lessons based on a carefully selected text.
During each unit, pupils explore the meaning, vocabulary and structure of the text before preparing it for performance. They learn how fluency, expression, pace, volume, intonation and gesture can help communicate meaning to an audience.Readers Theatre gives children opportunities to:• read and reread a text closely• develop accuracy, fluency and expression• explore vocabulary and meaning• discuss characters, themes and viewpoints• rehearse lines collaboratively• listen and respond to others• speak clearly and confidently• adapt their voice for purpose and audience• perform to their peers• reflect upon and improve a performance
The programme exposes children to a wide range of challenging material, including poetry, traditional texts, speeches, Shakespeare, diverse perspectives and texts containing figurative or symbolic language.
The selected texts also introduce pupils to features such as archaic language, complex narrators, non-linear sequences, symbolism, diverse perspectives and increasingly intricate plots. This helps children develop the confidence and knowledge needed to engage with more demanding texts.
Readers Theatre supports children who may be less confident readers by allowing them to rehearse and perform alongside others. It also provides appropriate challenge for fluent readers, who must consider interpretation, expression and how language should be communicated effectively.
Reading for pleasureWe want reading to be an enjoyable and valued part of everyday school life.Children have regular opportunities to:• choose books independently• visit the school library• listen to adults reading aloud• recommend books to one another• discuss authors and stories• explore unfamiliar genres and subjects• read at home and in school• celebrate their reading achievements
Our school library contains a wide range of current and engaging books. We hold regular DEAR sessions, which stands for Drop Everything and Read.
During these sessions, the whole school pauses to enjoy reading for pleasure in a calm and relaxed environment. The school library is also open during DEAR time, allowing children to return completed books and choose something new to read. These sessions help to build positive reading habits, encourage independence and ensure that children have regular opportunities to explore books that interest them.Accelerated ReaderWe use Accelerated Reader to support children’s independent reading.
Children complete regular assessments which help staff identify an appropriate reading range. They then choose books from within a personalised range, allowing them to experience success while gradually developing greater fluency, stamina and understanding.
After completing a book, children can take a short online quiz to check their comprehension and celebrate their progress. Accelerated Reader helps teachers monitor reading habits and identify pupils who may require additional support or challenge.
What Phonics looks like at St LaurencePhonics remains an important part of our reading provision for children who need additional support with decoding, fluency and spelling.
Every child’s phonics knowledge is assessed when they join St Laurence. Pupils who require further support follow Read Write Inc. Phonics or Fresh Start, which is designed specifically for older children who still need structured phonics teaching.
How we teach PhonicsChildren receive regular teaching in small, carefully organised groups. Sessions help pupils to:• recognise sounds and corresponding letters• blend sounds to read words• segment words for spelling• read increasingly fluently• understand what they have read• develop confidence as readers and writers
Progress is assessed regularly so that teaching and intervention can be matched closely to each child’s needs. Teaching and support staff receive training and regular refresher sessions in the delivery of Read Write Inc.
What Writing looks like at St LaurenceOur Writing curriculum enables children to communicate their ideas clearly, accurately and creatively.
Writing units are inspired by high-quality books, picture books, short stories and meaningful links with subjects such as Science and History. Each unit begins with an engaging stimulus which captures children’s interest and gives them a clear purpose for writing. Children write for a wide range of purposes and audiences, including to:• entertain• inform• explain• persuade• describe• discuss• recount
They learn that effective writing involves planning, drafting, revising, editing and presenting rather than completing a piece in one attempt.
How we teach WritingWriting is taught through a carefully structured sequence which helps children move from exploring ideas to producing an independent final outcome.
Our writing progression begins with explicit teaching of ambitious vocabulary and genre features. Children then explore sentence structures, plan their work, complete a first draft, edit and improve it before producing a final published version.
Children are encouraged to reread and edit as they write. Once the first draft is complete, they review the whole piece, improve vocabulary and respond to feedback before creating a carefully presented final copy.
Children consider the effectiveness of their writing and make changes to improve meaning, vocabulary, sentence structure and organisation.
What Grammar and Punctuation look like at St Laurence
Grammar and punctuation help children understand how language works and how meaning can be communicated clearly and effectively.
As children progress through Key Stage 2, they make increasingly deliberate grammatical choices to suit different audiences, purposes and forms of writing. They also learn to discuss language using accurate grammatical terminology.
At St Laurence, children develop secure knowledge of sentence structure, word classes, verb forms, punctuation and standard English. They learn to recognise these features in the texts they read and to use them accurately and purposefully in their own speaking and writing.
How we teach Grammar and PunctuationGrammar and punctuation are taught explicitly through regular, focused lessons using Spelling Shed resources. New concepts are introduced through clear explanations, modelling and worked examples before children practise and apply them independently.
Teaching is closely linked to reading and writing so that children understand how grammatical choices and punctuation affect meaning. Pupils explore examples from high-quality texts, discuss the effect of different sentence structures and then apply this learning within their own writing.
Lessons may include:• identifying and discussing grammatical features • practising new skills through short activities • improving and combining sentences • exploring how punctuation changes meaning • using accurate grammatical terminology • applying learning within a writing unit • proofreading and correcting errors • revisiting previous learning through regular retrieval practice
Grammar and punctuation are also embedded within each writing sequence. Children are taught the features most relevant to the genre they are studying, then expected to use them when planning, drafting, editing and improving their work.
What Spelling looks like at St LaurenceSpelling is taught systematically using Spelling Shed resources. Lessons develop children’s understanding of spelling patterns, phonics, morphology, word families and common exceptions.
Children are taught that spelling is not simply about memorising lists of words. They explore how words are constructed, recognise relationships between words and apply patterns and rules when encountering unfamiliar vocabulary.
How we teach SpellingSpelling teaching includes:• phonics and sound patterns• spelling rules and patterns• prefixes and suffixes• root words and word families• statutory words• commonly confused words• vocabulary and word meanings• proofreading and correcting errors• applying spelling knowledge within independent writing
New spelling patterns are introduced explicitly and practised through short, regular activities. Children are given opportunities to investigate words, identify similarities and explain the rules or patterns they notice.
Spelling Shed provides games, activities and resources which support learning in school and allow pupils to practise at home. Teachers use assessment and children’s independent writing to identify patterns which need to be revisited.
Pupils who require additional support with spelling may also receive targeted phonics teaching through Read Write Inc. Phonics or Fresh Start.
What Speaking and Listening look like at St LaurenceSpeaking and listening, or oracy, are developed throughout the English curriculum and across all areas of school life.
Children are taught to communicate their ideas clearly, listen attentively and respond appropriately to others. They are given regular opportunities to explain, question, discuss, debate, perform and present.
Readers Theatre makes a particularly strong contribution to oracy. Through rehearsing and performing texts, children learn how to use their voices effectively, respond to an audience and work collaboratively to communicate meaning.These experiences help pupils to:• develop confidence when speaking• organise and express their thoughts• listen carefully to different perspectives• build and use a rich vocabulary• give reasons for their opinions• ask relevant questions• adapt their speech for different audiences• contribute respectfully to discussions• rehearse ideas before writing• perform with fluency and expression
